episode_title: Address Poisoning Scams: The 30-Second Check Before Every Crypto Swap
summary: Erling joins Jules and Mira to break down lookalike swap sites, address poisoning, clipboard malware, fake support DMs and tampered hardware wallets, then walks through a five-step routine to verify a cross-chain swap before sending.
hook: One letter off in a domain. Matching first and last four characters in an address. That's all it took for two people to lose $62M combined. Security reviewer Erling explains how the most common cross-chain swap scams work and the boring 30-second habit that beats them.
key_points: How lookalike domains and sponsored ads lead to wallet-draining signatures ($6.27M from 4,741 victims in January 2026)
Why copying an address from your transaction history is exactly what address poisoning exploits
How clipboard malware swaps your pasted address, and why 'paste, then inspect' stops it
Why no real protocol DMs you first, and why a hardware wallet that arrives with a seed phrase is a red flag
A five-step pre-swap routine: verify the domain, check the full address, inspect the paste, send a test amount, track on an explorer like Chainflip Scan

chapters.title: Cold open: Dale's Diner vs Dale's Dinner
Clipboard malware and fake support DMs
The five-step routine before you send

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: [grinning] Okay, so at sixteen I bussed tables at Dale's Diner, out on Route 4. Best pie in the county. Rhubarb.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: This is going somewhere.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: It is! One spring a guy opens Dale's Dinner. Two n's. A quarter mile before ours, same red sign, and he puts up a billboard on the highway.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: [deadpan] Oh no.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Every tourist stops there first. Pie from a box. Then they drive on to us and yell at me about the pie.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: [amused] And somehow this is about crypto.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: It's about crypto, Mira.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Welcome to Cross-Chain Daily. I'm Mira, that's Jules, and today it's fake swap sites, address poisoning, and a simple routine to check a cross-chain swap before you hit send. Back with us on the security beat, Erling.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: [warmly] Hello again. For the record, I have never eaten a box pie on purpose.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Erling, how bad is this, really? Like, is it a few unlucky people?

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: Well, the article puts scam losses at about seventeen billion dollars in twenty twenty-five. And cross-chain swappers are some of the most targeted people out there.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: [stunned] Seventeen billion.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: With a B. Swapping across chains is fast, and scammers love fast. Fast means you don't look.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: So start with Jules's diner. Lookalike domains.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: Someone registers a domain that's one letter off the real swap site. A swapped letter, a hyphen. Then they buy an ad so it shows up first in search, or in your social feed.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: The billboard on the highway.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: [amused] Exactly the billboard. Except Dale's Dinner only took your lunch money. A fake swap site asks you to connect your wallet and sign something.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: And that signature is the drain.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: That's the drain. Signature phishing alone took six point two seven million dollars from four thousand seven hundred forty-one victims in January twenty twenty-six. Up two hundred seven percent from December.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: In one month? Two hundred percent?

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: [dryly] Two hundred and seven. I'm a stickler.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: So the fix is boring. Type the address yourself, or use a bookmark you made. Never click a swap link from an ad, a DM, or a search result without reading the whole domain.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Okay, honest question. Address poisoning. Sounds like someone put arsenic in my mailbox.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: [grinning] Close, honestly. You send to the same address a lot, so you copy it from your transaction history. Totally normal. Everyone does it.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: I do it.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: Of course you do. So an attacker makes an address with the same first and last characters as yours, and sends you a zero-value or dust transaction from it.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: So now it's sitting in your history, looking just like the real one.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: Right next to it. You glance at the first four and last four, they match, you paste, and you've paid the attacker.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: [quick, cutting in] Wait. They don't even need to hack anything?

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: Nothing. They just need you in a hurry. Two victims lost a combined sixty-two million dollars this way. One lost fifty million in December twenty twenty-five, another twelve point two million in January.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: The article's line is that these aren't edge cases. I believe it.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: [sheepish] Fifty million. I mean, I've never been that careful with fifty dollars.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: We know.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: So don't trust the first and last four. Expand the address and check the whole string. For a big transfer, cross-check it against another source, like a previous confirmed transaction on a block explorer.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: How do you, um, actually check forty-something characters without going cross-eyed?

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: I read it out loud in chunks of four, like a phone number. My cat thinks I'm reciting poetry.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: [deadpan] That's very calming, Erling.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: It is! Most relaxing part of my day.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Okay, what's clipboard malware? That one scares me more.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: It should, a little. It's software running quietly on your computer. It watches for you to copy a crypto address and swaps in the attacker's address instead.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: So I copy mine, I paste, uh, theirs.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: And everything looks normal. That's the nasty part. You only catch it if you compare the pasted address to the original, character by character.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Which is step three of the routine. Paste, then inspect.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: Clipboard malware depends on you not looking twice. So look twice.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: This is Dale's Dinner again. You think you pulled into the right lot.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: [half-laughing] Hmm. Right lot, but someone repainted the sign while you were parking.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: [groaning] Okay, that's worse and I hate it.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Next. Fake support DMs.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: Classic. You post on Discord, Telegram or X that your swap is stuck. Minutes later, support slides into your messages. They want you to connect to a verification tool, or share your seed phrase.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: [disbelieving] And people do it?

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: Impersonation scams grew more than fourteen hundred percent year over year in twenty twenty-five, partly thanks to AI-generated personas that look very convincing.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: So the rule is simple.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: No real protocol will ever DM you first. None will ask for your seed phrase. Treat every message you didn't ask for as hostile.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Like the waitress from Dale's Dinner knocking on my door, offering to fix my pie.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: [amused] Fine. That one's going in the spreadsheet. Entry twelve, Held up.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: [triumphant] Twelve!

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: Now the one that surprises people. Hardware wallets.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: I thought those were the safe part.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: [gently] They are, if the box is honest. On October twenty-ninth, twenty twenty-six, Singapore police warned that some Ledger devices sold through local stores had been tampered with. They came with seed phrases already set by attackers.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: How much was lost?

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: Two cases, about three point five million Singapore dollars, roughly two point seven million US, since September tenth.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: So the, the safe was built by the burglar.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: [amused] Pretty much. Buy only from the maker's official site or authorized resellers. Check the packaging. Your device should make a fresh seed phrase during setup. If it arrives with one already written down, stop. Right there.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Let's run the whole routine, quickly. One.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: Verify the domain. Type it, or use your own bookmark.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Two.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: Compare the full address, not just the ends.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Three, paste, then look twice.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: Four, on anything big, send a test amount. Wait for it to confirm, check you can access it at the other end, then send the rest. The extra network fee is cheap insurance.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: [half-laughing] I used to think test amounts were for nervous people.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: They are. Be nervous. And five, track it on an explorer. Chainflip Scan, for example, follows a swap from deposit to final settlement, with the exact output address and amount received.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: And the article's big point is that speed is the enemy here.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: [easy] Scammers count on urgency and habit. Thirty extra seconds to check a domain, read an address, or send a test can save you from losing everything.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Thirty seconds. Those tourists could've saved a whole lunch.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: Takeaway: slow down just enough. Domain, full address, the paste, a test, then track it. The full article is linked in the show notes. Not financial advice.

lines.speaker: erling
lines.text: And read your addresses out loud. Your cat will love it.

lines.speaker: jules
lines.text: Stay native.

lore.note: At sixteen he bussed tables at Dale's Diner on Route 4 (famous rhubarb pie). A copycat 'Dale's Dinner' with two n's opened a quarter mile earlier with the same red sign and a highway billboard, served box pie, and tourists yelled at Jules about it. His picture of lookalike swap domains and malicious ads.
Checks crypto addresses by reading them out loud in chunks of four like a phone number; his cat thinks he's reciting poetry, and he calls it the most relaxing part of his day.
Jules's 'Dale's Dinner waitress knocking on your door offering to fix your pie' (fake support DMs) became entry twelve in the 'Held up' column of her spreadsheet.
